findings.quote: The predictive power of the EEG features to identify the classroom design condition was specific to the cognitive test performed. When the participants were engaged in the VMT, the classifier could identify any of the three design conditions compared to the Neutral classroom with statistically significant success (p < 0.003). Specifically, the test-set median classification accuracies for the three design conditions evaluated were: 55.0% Neutral vs One-Window, 61.3% Neutral vs Two-Windows, 61.3% Neutral vs One-Window. The classifier also distinguished, significantly higher than chance (p < 0.003), the design conditions evaluated for the Benton Test in the Neutral vs One-Window comparison, and in the Neutral vs Two-Windows comparison; with test-set median classification accuracies of 61.3% and 56.3%, respectively.

findings.quote: It is notable that this outcome is not consistent with previous work that has found, for example, views of nature to be associated with improved working memory and decreased mental fatigue (Bratman et al., 2015; Gladwell et al., 2012; Li & Sullivan, 2016). One possible explanation for these contradictory results may be the length of exposure. Kaplan's (1995) Attention Restoration Theory and Ulrich and colleagues (1991) Stress Reduction Theory both propose that the beneficial effects of nature enable involve the attentuation of certain cognitive, affective, and physiological functions—e.g. directed attention (Kaplan), or stress response of the sympathetic nervous system (Ulrich and colleagues)—resulting from time spent viewing nature. In the current study, participants remained in each virtual classroom for less than two minutes and were constantly under mild stress while completing the cognitive tests. Thus, there may not have been enough contemplative time for the window views to have a restorative effect.

limitations: Small sample size (n=23) increases likelihood of Type II error; majority were university students with high computer experience
Sample demographics: majority university students with prior VR experience; may limit generalizability to other populations
Gender may moderate VR responses; prior studies show males and gamers perform better in VR environments
Short exposure duration (1-2 minutes per condition) may be insufficient to trigger sustained attention restoration effects
Cognitive tests are well-validated but implications for long-term learning outcomes unclear
Virtual reality environment may not fully capture real-world architectural features (e.g., ambient noise, temperature dynamics, natural light variation)
'Ceiling effect': participants scored nearly perfectly on many tasks, limiting cognitive demand and possible restorative effects of design
Causality cannot be definitively established; neural features may correlate with rather than cause performance differences

overall_theory_links.relevance: Window views with natural scenery may restore directed attention, but short exposure duration (1-2 min) may be insufficient
Natural views expected to reduce stress and enhance cognition, but effects not observed in short VR sessions with concurrent cognitive task stress

EEG classifier found larger effects for tasks requiring sustained stimulus presentation in memory (DST, BT, VMT) vs switching attention (Stroop, Arithmetic); supports context-dependent memory encoding
Connectivity changes from centroparietal to frontal cortex suggest task-specific integration of information processing during architectural design manipulation

study_strengths: Rigorous machine learning approach with leave-one-out cross-validation provides robust generalization assessment
Comprehensive EEG feature extraction: 285 frequency band-power features + 3920 connectivity features
Bonferroni-corrected statistical thresholds (p < 0.003, p < 0.0006 for multiple comparisons) control for Type I error
Scrambled baseline control data confirms that results are not due to chance
Multiple cognitive tests allow task-specific neural effects to emerge
Precise architectural variable manipulation in VR (window placement, room dimensions) isolates design effects from confounds
study_limitations: No significant behavioral effects on cognitive performance despite significant EEG differences—suggests design effects are subtle or task-specific
Short exposure duration limits ecological validity of findings
VR may not fully replicate real-world architectural experience
High participant VR experience may bias results toward positive VR engagement
Relatively small sample limits statistical power for some comparisons
key_methodological_notes.statistical_approach: Non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis tests at significance thresholds p < 0.05 and p < 0.01 for behavioral data; machine learning classification with Kruskal-Wallis feature selection and Bonferroni correction (p < 0.01 for 4205 features) for EEG data
key_methodological_notes.eeg_analysis_pipeline: Raw EEG (500 Hz) → bandpass filter 0.5-50 Hz (FIR Hamming window) → artifact subspace reconstruction → independent component analysis → feature extraction (frequency band-power and PDC connectivity) → Kruskal-Wallis feature ranking → k-SVM classification → leave-one-out cross-validation
